name: Kopczyński-Trautman Universe With Torsion
description: A flat universe of dust whose particles all spin about one axis, in the Einstein-Cartan theory, where the spin of matter gives spacetime torsion as its energy gives it curvature. The spins repel at high density, so the universe contracts to a least size, turns round, and expands, with no singularity. W. Kopczyński found the first such universes in 1972 and 1973, and Andrzej Trautman argued from them in 1973 that spin and torsion may avert gravitational singularities.
convention: The length $\ell = c/\sqrt{6\pi G\rho_0}$ sets every scale, with $\rho_0$ the mass density of the dust at $t = 0$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$, of the Christoffel connection, which carries no torsion.
history: Élie Cartan let spacetime twist as well as curve in 1922, before anyone knew that the electron spins [trautman2006, cartan1923]. He had in mind the elastic medium of the brothers Cosserat, whose points can each be turned as well as moved, and in his theory the spin of matter is the source of a twist in the geometry, its torsion, as energy is the source of curvature [hehl2007, trautman2006]. For more than thirty years the theory attracted no attention, and Dennis Sciama and T. W. B. Kibble had each found it again by 1961 [trautman2006, kibble1961, hehl2007]. Wherever terms quadratic in the spin can be neglected the theory is general relativity, and those terms amount to a contact force between spins, which Kibble judged "almost certainly too small to make any experimentally detectable difference" [trautman2006, kibble1961]. "If the history had been reversed and the spin of the electron discovered before 1915", Sciama said in 1979, "I have little doubts that Einstein would have wanted to include torsion in his original formulation of general relativity" [hehl2007].¶Isotropic models of the universe, Andrzej Trautman wrote in 1973, "lead to the prediction of at least one moment in the history of the Universe with an infinite density of matter" [trautman1973]. The symmetry was suspected at first: "for some time it was thought that the singularities might be a consequence of the high symmetry of the models" [trautman1973]. The theorems of Roger Penrose and Stephen Hawking need no symmetry: gravity that attracts, which is an energy condition on the matter, a well behaved causal structure, and one thing more, such as a closed trapped surface, are enough for a singularity [penrose1965, hawkingpenrose1970, senovilla1998]. Is there a way out that keeps ordinary matter? With torsion in the theory the spins add a term of their own to the source of gravity, and the total "need not satisfy the positive energy conditions" even where the matter does [trautman2006].¶In Warsaw, W. Kopczyński tried it on a universe: his spherically symmetric cloud of spinning dust, published in 1972, gave "a two-parameter family of world-models without singularities of the Friedmann type" [kopczynski1972]. The simplest such universe is his of 1973: flat space filled with dust at rest, every particle spinning about the same axis [kopczynski1973, trautman2006]. Its scale factor is $a = (1 + c^2t^2/\ell^2)^{1/3}$, with $\ell$ a length set by the dust's greatest density [trautman2006]. Far from $t = 0$ that is $a \propto t^{2/3}$, the scale factor of Friedmann's flat universe of dust [trautman2006]. Near $t = 0$ the spins hold the dust apart: their term in Friedmann's equation is "a repulsive potential, effective at small values" of the scale factor, and "it prevents the solution from vanishing" [trautman2006]. The universe contracts, stops at $a = 1$, and expands again, with its curvature finite at every moment [trautman2006].¶How small does it get? Trautman put numbers in: a universe of about $10^{80}$ nucleons with every spin aligned, an assumption he called unrealistic, turns round at a radius of about one centimetre [trautman2006]. Its density there is of the order of $10^{55}$ grams per cubic centimetre, very large, and still some thirty eight powers of ten below the Planck density, where quantum gravity is believed to take over [trautman2006]. The turn comes where the mass density $\rho$ and the spin density $\sigma$ satisfy $\rho c^4 = 2\pi G\sigma^2$: the repulsion of the spins grows as $1/a^6$ while the density of the dust grows as $1/a^3$, so the spins dominate at small $a$ [trautman2006, poplawski2010].¶The objection came in August 1973 from John Stewart and Peter Hájíček: "the singularity is avoided only because of the high symmetry of the model used" [stewart1973]. Kopczyński had already found as much in a flat universe free to expand at different rates in different directions, where the bounce survives only "if the effect of torsion is greater than that of shear" [kopczynski1973]. Even a very small shear counteracts the repulsion of the spins [trautman2006]. By 1974 the singularity theorems had been carried over to the theory with torsion by Friedrich Hehl, Paul von der Heyde, and G. David Kerlick, who found that every model then known to avoid a singularity violates an energy condition [hehl1974]. Kerlick then traded the spinning dust for a Dirac field, and the effect reversed: there the interaction between spins "enhances rather than opposes singularity formation" [kerlick1975]. The work of those years is gathered in the review by Hehl, von der Heyde, Kerlick, and James Nester [hehl1976, trautman2006].¶What if the spins point at random? Terms quadratic in the spin remain after the averaging, and with them, Bronisław Kuchowicz found in 1978, the Friedmann universes carry over to the theory, isotropic and free of singularity [kuchowicz1978]. The bounce came back in 2010, when Nikodem Popławski filled a closed universe with quarks and leptons, found that it turns round at a radius of $9 \times 10^{-6}$ m, and proposed it as an alternative to inflation [poplawski2010]. He suggested that the contraction before the bounce is the collapse of a black hole in another universe [poplawski2010]. Trautman's own summary, in 2006, was that the theory "differs very slightly from the Einstein theory", its effects significant "only at densities of matter that are very high, but nevertheless much smaller than the Planck density" [trautman2006].

related.text: The same line element with the scale factor left free. This universe is the flat one whose scale factor solves Friedmann's equation with the repulsion of the spins added to it [trautman2006].

Another universe that contracts, turns round, and expands with no singularity. Senovilla's is a solution of general relativity that keeps the energy conditions and has no closed trapped surface, and this one violates an energy condition through the spin of its dust [chinea1992, hehl1974].

Homogeneous universes that expand at different rates in different directions. Filled with spinning dust in the Einstein-Cartan theory, universes of Bianchi types I to VIII can avoid the singularity too, where the torsion outweighs the shear [tafel1973, kopczynski1973].

Spin as a source of gravity along a line. Harald Soleng built a cosmic string in the Einstein-Cartan theory in 1992, its spin polarised along its axis, with the spinning string's spacetime outside it [soleng1992].

coordinates.name: Comoving Cartesian

parameters.description: Length that sets every scale, $\ell = c/\sqrt{6\pi G\rho_0}$, with $\rho_0$ the mass density of the dust at $t = 0$, where it is greatest; the spin density there is $\sigma_0 = c^2\sqrt{\rho_0/2\pi G}$
Scale factor, least at $t = 0$, where $a = 1$; the mass density is $\rho_0/a^3$ and the spin density $\sigma_0/a^3$

coordinates.convention: We use Trautman's coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, at rest with the dust, with $t$ its proper time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths measured at $t = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Comoving Spherical

parameters.description: Length that sets every scale, $\ell = c/\sqrt{6\pi G\rho_0}$, with $\rho_0$ the mass density of the dust at $t = 0$, where it is greatest; the spin density there is $\sigma_0 = c^2\sqrt{\rho_0/2\pi G}$
Scale factor, least at $t = 0$, where $a = 1$; the mass density is $\rho_0/a^3$ and the spin density $\sigma_0/a^3$

coordinates.convention: We use the proper time $t$ of the dust and a comoving radius $r$, the areal radius of the sphere through a point divided by $a$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal Time

parameters.description: Scale factor, the solution of $(\partial_\eta a)^2 = 4(a - a^{-2})/9\ell^2$ with $a = 1$ at $\eta = 0$, where it is least

coordinates.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$, a length with $a\,d\eta = c\,dt$ and $\eta = 0$ at $t = 0$, and the comoving radius $r$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
